content.title: All 7 Ties In Oscars History: Moments That Changed The Academy Awards
content.text: Advertisement Dismiss Ad Dismiss Adby Spencer AlthouseBuzzFeedBuzzFeed StaffI’m the Editorial Director at BuzzFeed — where I’ve reported on TV, film, and lifestyle trends (travel, fitness, and food) since 2013 — and I also post about the latest in pop culture news to my 850k+ followers on TikTok. 1/1 Skip Ad Continue watchingafter the adVisit Advertiser websiteGO TO PAGE In the last 98 years of Academy Awards history, there have actually been seven different ties, the most recent happening at the 2026 Oscars! Two of those ties have even happened in the acting categories. Some Oscar ties resulted in a ton of drama, while others led to a complete overhaul of the rules. Here they are, in order. Enjoy! 1. The first tie occurred in the Best Actor category at the 5th Oscars ceremony in 1932, and it literally forced the Academy to change its rules. Fredric March (Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde) and Wallace Beery (The Champ) both won, but technically Fredric had received one more vote than Wallace. At the time, the rules stated that anyone who came within three votes of the winner would also be awarded the prize, so they each took home a statue that night. John Kobal Foundation / Getty Images Here are Fredric March (on the right) and Wallace Beery (on the left) at their ceremony, Oscars in hand. Advertisement Wildly enough, only three actors were nominated in that category to begin with, meaning everyone won except Alfred Lunt (The Guardsman). After this happened, the Academy made it so only "true" ties with the same exact number of votes would count. MGM, Paramount Pictures 2. The next tie occurred in 1950 in the Best Documentary Short category. There were four nominees that year, and the two shortest films won: So Much for So Little and A Chance to Live. ABC / youtube.com Advertisement So Much for So Little is a 10-minute animated short about the importance of healthcare and public health agencies (it was actually commissioned by the US government and made by Warner Bros. Cartoons, so, like, it's literally part of the Looney Tunes collection now). Meanwhile, A Chance to Live is an 18-minute short about an Irish priest and the institution he founded for orphaned boys who were displaced after World War II. Heavy stuff! Warner Bros. Cartoons 3. The third tie occurred in 1969, and it's easily the most famous tie in Oscars history. The category was Best Actress, and both Katharine Hepburn (The Lion in Winter) and onscreen newcomer Barbra Streisand (Funny Girl) had their names announced. However, there's a bit of drama here, so let's get into it! ABC Advertisement Okay, so Barbra Streisand originated the role of Fanny Brice in Funny Girl on Broadway in 1964, resulting in her second Tony nomination. She then reprised that character in her first-ever movie role in the 1968 adaptation. This obviously led to Barbra tying with Kate at the Oscars, but that's only because she was invited to join the Academy early by then-president Gregory Peck. This was very controversial! Silver Screen Collection / Getty Images, John Bryson / Getty Images Normally, each new Academy member has to meet certain criteria to be invited into the voting body. For example, at the time, one way was for applicants to appear in at least three major films (remember: Funny Girl was Barbra's first movie!). The other way to be inducted is to literally win or get nominated for an Oscar, as it's tradition for all new winners and nominees to join the year ~after~ their ceremony takes place. Again, though, this rare exception for Barbra was made, presumably allowing her to vote for herself, forcing a tie. A ton of people were upset and even called out Gregory Peck, claiming that Barbra was only rushed into membership due to "studio politics or pressure," which he "categorically rejected." The Hollywood Reporter / hollywoodreporter.com, Fotos International / Getty Images In a 1969 clipping from the Hollywood Reporter, Gregory Peck said, “There is no studio pressure in any phase of the Academy’s activities. There are loyalties and advocacies, of course, but pressure, no. It’s impossible. We’re not dependent on the studios. We’re not under any obligation to them. They have no leverage at all on the Academy.” Advertisement Anyway, all of this resulted in Barbra and Kate receiving exactly 3,030 votes each, so they both took home awards that night. Because of this, Kate actually became the second actress in history to win back-to-back Oscars, having won the previous year for Guess Who's Coming to Dinner. This was her third of four acting Oscars, a record that has still never been broken. This win also helped Barbra Streisand EGOT the following year, though technically it's a non-competitive EGOT since her Tony was a special "Star of the Decade" award. ABC The above photo is from Kate Hepburn's only appearance in Academy Awards history. It was in 1974, and she presented Lawrence Weingarten with the Irving G. Thalberg Memorial Award. Upon approaching the stage, she joked, "I am very happy that I didn't hear anyone call out 'it's about time!'" 4. The next tie occurred in 1987 in the Best Documentary (Feature) category. There were five nominees, and the two winners were Artie Shaw: Time Is All You've Got and Down and Out in America. ABC Advertisement That latter doc was actually directed by four-time Supporting Actress nominee (and one-time winner for 1975's Shampoo) Lee Grant. Now, technically, no one has ever won both an Acting and Directing Oscar, but Lee Grant certainly comes the closest. By today's rules, she would have won the 1987 Oscar for directing this documentary, but back then the award went to the film's producer (so her husband actually won it instead...typical!). Anyway, Lee Grant is incredible, so go watch her movies. She's also still alive today, having turned 100 back in October! ABC 5. The fifth tie occurred in 1995, this time in the Best Live-Action Short Film category. Five movies were nominated, and the two winners were Trevor and Franz Kafka's It's a Wonderful Life. ABC Advertisement Wildly enough, Franz Kafka's It's a Wonderful Life was actually written and directed by actor Peter Capaldi. You probably know him best as the Twelfth Doctor in Doctor Who or the British comedy series The Thick of It. ABC / BBC 6. Up until the 2026 Oscars, the most recent tie occurred in 2013 in the Sound Editing Category. Of the five films nominated, the two winners were Zero Dark Thirty (Paul N. J. Ottosson) and Skyfall (Per Hallberg and Karen Baker Landers). ABC Advertisement Mark Wahlberg presented the award. Upon announcing that there was a tie, the audience gasped, and he responded, "No B.S.!" ABC 7. And finally, at the most recent Oscars ceremony, there was a tie in the Live-Action Short Film category. The two winners were The Singers and Two People Exchanging Saliva. ABC Advertisement Kumail Nanjiani presented the award and rightfully freaked out when he saw the winning names on the envelope. The entire audience gasped, which was super thrilling. Then, after the first winner gave their speech, Kumail jumped in with this unscripted joke: "It's ironic that the Short Film Oscar is gonna take twice as long." ABC So thrilling! Here's to more Oscar ceremonies, movie magic, and watching people's dreams come true. Comments❤️8👍4🙄2😂😭🤯😡😬Top CommentCowboys2212 days agoMar 14, 20264:50 pmSo if they tie?
